chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub said: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazi', from Hanan ibn Sudayr, from his father, who said:
Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'A prescribed punishment (hadd) which is established in the earth is more purifying therein than the rain of forty nights and days.'

key_terms.أَزْكَى: more purifying/more wholesome — comparative form of zakiy (pure, righteous); carries connotations of both spiritual and physical purity
key_terms.حَدٌّ: Hadd — a category of fixed, divinely prescribed punishment in Islamic law for specific crimes (e.g., theft, adultery, slander)
key_terms.يُقَامُ: is established/carried out — from the root q-w-m, meaning to stand upright, to establish, to carry out

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Baqir say about the purifying effect of implementing hadd punishments?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) teaches that the implementation of a divinely prescribed legal punishment (hadd) has a greater purifying effect on society than forty days and nights of rain. The statement uses the Arabic root z-k-w (زكو), meaning both spiritual and material purification, to draw a vivid comparison between physical rain that cleanses the earth and the socio-spiritual cleansing that comes from upholding divine law. In the context of early Islamic jurisprudence, this teaching emphasized to the community that enforcing hudud was not merely punitive but served a profound purificatory and restorative function for the social body.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yaqoub, from Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Isa, from Muhammad Bin Isnail Bin Bazie, from Hanan Bin Sudeyr, from his father who said,
Abu Ja’farasws said: ‘A Limit (Hadd) which is established in the earth is more purifying therein than the rain of forty nights and days’.
